meta.title: Early Detection of Satellite Telemetry Data Anomalies using Hyperdimensional Computing
meta.authorsHtml: Benjamin Scott<sup>∗</sup><sup>1,2</sup>, Tajana Rosing<sup>1</sup>, Flavio Ponzina<sup>2</sup>

abstract: Spacecraft operations depend on continuous telemetry streams to assess subsystem health, yet most anomaly detectors are reactive, raising alarms only after anomalous samples appear. We present SatAnomHD, a prediction-driven pipeline for early detection of satellite telemetry anomalies using hyperdimensional computing (HDC). SatAnomHD encodes each telemetry channel with permutation–level hypervectors that preserve temporal order and continuous values, and trains a multivariate HDC autoregressor to forecast S future samples per channel. Predicted trajectories are re-encoded via random projection and scored by a lightweight binary HDC classifier to estimate anomaly probability within a tunable horizon, providing tens-ofseconds to minutes of lead time. HDC learning uses simple, gradient-free operations with incremental updates, enabling efficient inference and on-board finetuning under CubeSat-class power and memory limits. We evaluate SatAnomHD on the ESA Anomaly Detection Benchmark (ESA- ADB), Mission1, spanning 14 years of operations. Across horizons from 30 s to 5 min ahead, SatAnomHD matches the alarm precision of the current state of the art while delivering up to 60×/230× faster and 56×/206× more energy-efficient inference/training, shifting detection from reactive scoring to predictive early warning.

blocks.html: Spacecraft operations teams rely on continuous telemetry streams to assess subsystem health and safety [1]. Anomaly detection in these multivariate time series is mission-critical: missed events can escalate into failures, while false alarms increase operator workload. The challenge is intensifying with greater spacecraft autonomy and complexity, constellation-scale data volumes, and reduced ground visibility due to intermittent contacts, limited bandwidth, and deep-space latency [2]. These trends motivate methods that are both accurate and deployable, including on-board inference and adaptation to evolving regimes. Machine-learning detectors typically learn nominal behavior and flag anomalies via reconstruction residuals or window-level classification [3]. Standardized evaluation has also improved: ESA-ADB provides real telemetry, expert annotations, and an operations-aligned protocol [4]. Yet existing telemetry anomaly detectors remain reactive, triggering only after anomalous samples are observed or fall within the analysis window. In mission operations, however, lead time is as important as accuracy, enabling proactive actions (mode change, load shedding, isolation, targeted diagnostics). Most prior telemetry approaches compute residuals against the next measurement, while window-based classifiers require the anomaly signature to be present in the observation window [5, 6]. Even more advanced time-series anomaly detection methods proposed for IoT and industrial IoT settings [7–11] remain essentially reactive, declaring anomalies only after the relevant samples are observed.

This paper targets early detection of satellite telemetry anomalies by estimating whether an anomaly is likely within a future horizon before the corresponding telemetry is sampled. We propose SatAnomHD, a lightweight, prediction-driven pipeline for satellite telemetry anomaly detection using hyperdimensional computing (HDC). Our key contribution combines: (i) a multivariate HDC forecaster that predicts a short future telemetry trajectory from recent history and (ii) an HDC classifier that uses these predictions to estimate anomaly likelihood within a tunable horizon. By classifying predictions rather than waiting for measurements, SatAnomHD provides explicit pre-sampling lead time and a trade-off between warning horizon (tens of seconds to minutes) and false alarms. HDC also fits on-board energy constraints for both inference and training: unlike space-AI pipelines such as DC-VAE [12] and Telenamom-ESA [13] that rely on deep models that are costly to retrain or adapt in flight, our method supports gradient-free, incremental updates with small memory and low energy cost, enabling continual refinement under new environments and slow distribution shifts on ultra-low-power CubeSat-class hardware [14, 15]. Experimental results show that the SatAnomHD matches anomaly-detection performance of state-of-the-art approaches, while delivering up to 60×/230× faster and 56×/206× more energy-efficient inference/training. Crucially, SatAnomHD shifts anomaly detection from reactive monitoring to predictive early alerts.

Anomaly detection algorithms. Time-series anomaly detection has progressed from classical statistical and unsupervised methods like OCSVM [16], Isolation Forest [17], and Local Outlier Factor [18], that flag deviations from expected temporal behavior, to deep learning models, with reconstruction-based encoder–decoder algorithms like LSTM-AE [19] and Transformer families [20, 21] which learn normal representations and detect anomalies via reconstruction error. In parallel, generative/adversarial models like USAD [22] learn nominal distributions, and contrastive self-supervised methods such as DCdetector [10] and TS2Vec [11] learn robust temporal features. However, these models are not currently used in space applications because of their prohibitive resource requirements [2, 23].

Spacecraft telemetry anomaly detection. Telemetry anomaly detection spans rule-based limits, model-based residual tests, and data-driven ML [4]. Recent work increasingly uses deep architectures to capture temporal dependencies and cross-channel interactions. An edgeoriented study on ESA-ADB shows strong event-wise performance and explores neural architecture optimization to reduce memory/compute for constrained deployment [24]. Prior work on ML methods for space applications emphasizes energy/performance characterization of resource-efficient paradigms, radiation-hardened processors, and the need for in-flight updates under realistic hardware assumptions [25]. Space edge-AI studies show deep detectors can be compressed to small memory footprints while retaining performance [24]. Other efforts address irregular sampling, such as temporal-enhanced transformers that encode non-uniform time gaps [26], and explainability methods that support operator diagnosis [27]. ESA-ADB enables reproducible comparisons with operator-relevant metrics [4], but the considered approaches, as well as the general anomaly detection algorithms discussed above, still do not provide pre-sampling lead time because they depend on observed measurements to score residuals.

Early warning and on-board deployability. Energy-efficient regressors are pivotal to enable early warning for real-world satellite applications. Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) emerged as a promising alternative to deep models in space applications due to its limited memory requirements, high compute parallelism, and efficient inference/training operations [28]. Prior HDC work [29–33] shows how to perform time series regression in the HDC domain. Nonetheless, the best performing methods (e.g., RegHD [29] and KalmanHD [30]) are limited to simple univariate IoT datasets and only offer a single-sample prediction horizon, hence preventing long-term predictions.

Overview. SatAnomHD, summarized in Fig. 1, integrates a multivariate HDC regressor with a window-based HDC classifier to enable early detection of telemetry anomalies in satellite operations. Each input modality is first encoded in a high-dimensional space using a combination of permutation and level encoding (Fig. 1-A). Next, the proposed HDC autoregressor predicts S future samples for each modality (Fig. 1-B), representing the key step to enable early detection of anomalous events. These predicted samples are then mapped back in a high-dimensional space (Fig. 1-C), where a binary HDC classifier is used to detect anomalies in the predicted future samples (Fig. 1-D).

Multivariate HDC Encoding. We propose a novel encoding method to map multivariate telemetry samples into a high-dimensional space. Our encoding function uses similar element-wise operations used for time-series encoding as in [29, 31, 34, 35], but is extended in this work to multivariate time-series regression. Additionally, it substitutes feature encoding based on ID vectors with a level-based encoding method [36] that better maps the continuous data range of telemetry data. In this initial phase, each telemetry channel ci ∈{c0, c1, . . . , cM} is treated independently, and the last measured N samples of each channel are used to form M time series windows wj used to include temporal information in the HDC domain and maps each window wi into a corresponding HV as corresponding to the scalar value wk tor rotation of k elements. Unlike prior multivariate HDC classification approaches that aggregate channel information into a unified representation [37] for classification tasks, SatAnomHD uses the resulting hypervectors HVi as inputs to a multivariate HDC regressor that predicts S future samples for each channel.

blocks.html: Autoregressive Forecasting. Compared to the single-channel HDC-based regressor in [29], our model improves in three ways. First, it supports multivariate inputs and produces c-dimensional outputs. Second, it enables longterm forecasting: rather than predicting only one future sample per time series, each prediction is fed back to form new multivariate windows that mix past measured samples with the current predicted sample, yielding up to S predicted samples per channel and enabling anomaly assessment without requiring future measurements, unlike prior work. Third, it improves training via a Kalman-style update [30], increasing prediction accuracy. It also binarizes representations and uses a diagonal approximation of the error-covariance matrix P, keeping only per-dimension variances as p ∈RD instead of a full D × D matrix. This is justified by the near-orthogonality of high-dimensional random bipolar vectors, which makes off-diagonal covariances vanish in expectation for large D, and is further strengthened by binarization: (hi)2 = 1 element-wise, making the Kalman gain computation diagonal without approximation error.

Projection HDC Encoding. The regressor output Y is a (M, S) matrix including the predicted S samples for each of the M considered telemetry channels. Each prethen mapped back in the HDC domain using simple binary random projection encoding, hence treating each channel information equally.

HDC Anomaly Detection. Finally, the encoded features are fed into a simple binary HDC classifier that evaluates whether the predicted samples correspond to a telemetry anomaly or not using a typical HDC pipeline. To allow trade-offs between detection accuracy and a reduced number of false alarms, we design SatAnomHD to trigger an alert only when the cosine similarity between the query HV and the class HV corresponding to anomaly data exceeds a tunable threshold τ ∈(0, 1).

On-board continual model fine-tuning. While training deep models requires extensive energy (2−5×), compute (2−4×), and memory (3−10×) overhead, training HDC models only requires the same element-wise vector operations such as additions and multiplications used during the inference stage. Hence, our proposed approach leverages the lightweight nature of HDC training to enable on-board model finetuning, crucial to adapt the regressor and classifier based on the actual collected data. The regressor is updated fully online, sample-by-sample, requiring no replay buffer, gradients, or passes over historical data, using Kalman filter theory to implement noise-resilient updates. It maintains three state variables: the per-channel weight hypervectors α ∈RM×D, the shared diagonal covariance p ∈RD, and a measurement-noise estimate σ2. At time t, after observing the actual sample yt ∈RM, the per-channel error innovation error (prediction error) the shared binary hypervector encoding the current window. The update is skipped if At = maxc |E(c, t)| ≤0.1, where At is the l∞innovation norm, following the threshold of [30], preventing noisy updates during quiet periods. Otherwise, the intermediate vector mt = pt ⊙ht, projects the covariance onto the observed direction, and the scalar uncertainty dt = ht · mt + σ2 the Kalman gain denominator. The Kalman gain is Gt = mt/dt ∈RD, shared across channels, and the weights are updated channel-wise as αc,t+1 = αc,t + ηEc,tGt for c ∈1, . . . , M, where η is the fixed learning rate. The covariance updates as pt+1 = pt −Gt ⊙mt + q, where the process noise scalar q > 0 prevents collapse, and sustains adaptation under distribution drift. Measurement noise is smoothed via σ2 γ ∈(0, 1) is the smoothing coefficient. This causal recurrence keeps a fixed memory footprint, storing only α, p, and σ2. Finally, the HDC classifier can also be retrained on-board using the collected samples following [38].

blocks.html: Experimental Setup. We evaluate SatAnomHD on the ESA-ADB dataset [4], which contains real-world telemetry from multiple space missions. All experiments use the Mission1 subset (over 3.5 GB collected across 14 years of operations). SatAnomHD uses a 3,000-dimensional hyperspace: regressor and classifier HVs use integer representations and are ℓ2-normalized after training, while encoding HVs use bipolar values in {−1, +1}. We consider prediction horizons of S = {1, 5, 10} samples, enabling early anomaly detection from 30 s to 5 min ahead. The classifier margin threshold used to raise an anomaly detection alert is set to τ = 0.2. We set our training configuration to be the following: N = 5, D = 5, |L| = 512, B = 64, η = 0.001, γ = 0.0002, p0 = 0.1, and q = 0.00001. We compare against the best-performing ESA-ADB baselines reported in prior work: Global-STD [39], DC-VAE-ESA based on [12], and Telemanom-ESA [13]. For a fair comparison with [4], we report precision, recall, F0.5, alarming precision, and anomaly detection timing quality curve (ADTQC). We evaluate runtime and energy on CubeSat-representative HW platforms [14, 15]. Experiments are run in Pytorch for accuracy experiments and in C, where SatAnomHD leverages multi-threading and SIMD for performance improvements.

Autoregressive forecaster. Fig 2 illustrates a qualitative overview of the predictive performance of the implemented regressor for 500 samples collected over six channels during 15 minutes of satellite operations. Experimental results show that SatAnomHD achieves MAE of 0.20, 0.23, 0.26, and 0.32 at horizons S = {1, 3, 5, 10}, respectively. MAE increases by only 0.12 over a 10× harder prediction task (i.e., from S = 1 to S = 10), reflecting graceful degradation rather than catastrophic error compounding across horizons.

Anomaly detection. Table 1 compares SatAnomHD against established baselines across prediction horizons S ∈{1, 5, 10}. Telenamom-ESA achieves top accuracy across the different considered metrics, while SatAnomHD offers comparable or better precision, recall, and F0.5 compared to Global-STD and DC-VAE-ESA, while matching the alarm precision of Telenamom-ESA and offering lead times up to 5 minutes.

Performance results. Table 2 evaluates the different solutions in terms of inference and training performance. Despite delivering high precision and recall, Telemanom- ESA exhibits large inference and training time. The proposed SatAnomHD achieves inference/training speedups of up to 60× and 231×, respectively, reducing energy cost by a similar factor (56× and 206×).

The modest multi-horizon degradation of the proposed regressor (only 0.12 from S=1 to S=10) highlights the stability of Kalman-style updates, which limit error amplification during autoregressive rollout. Relative to KalmanHD [30], SatAnomHD provides (i) multivariate regression, (ii) multi-step autoregressive prediction for early anomaly detection, and (iii) a diagonal-P covariance approximation that cuts per-sample update complexity from O(d2) to O(d). Its alarm precision substantially exceeds Global-STD and DC- VAE-ESA (∼25×), reducing false alarms while matching the output quality of Telemanom-ESA. Compared to this high-accuracy baseline, SatAnomHD lowers inference and training costs by 25×–230× via lightweight element-wise operations. We also analyze the effect of the threshold τ on alarm precision and the precision–recall trade-off. τ selects an operating point on the precision–recall frontier, allowing operators to tune risk tolerance without retraining. Low thresholds (τ ∈[0.1, 0.2]) trigger earlier and more often, improving event recall but reducing precision; higher thresholds (τ ∈[0.25, 0.3], used in Table 1) suppress spurious alarms and push precision toward conservative baselines such as Telemanom-ESA, at the expense of recall for borderline events. Notably, F0.5 peaks and remains stable for τ ∈[0.18, 0.22], indicating robustness and supporting τ=0.2 as a natural operating point rather than a cherry-picked optimum. Finally, Table 2 shows that HDC retraining uses the same element-wise operations as inference, enabling on-board fine-tuning within Cube- Sat power budgets. The True Negative Rate (TNR) is the fraction of nominal samples correctly left unflagged; it governs the false positive rate and dominates precisionweighted F0.5. Extending training history from 10 to 42 months raises TNR from 0.97 to 0.99 and reduces false positive events from 300 to 117, increasing SatAnomHD F0.5 by 0.123. Because HDC updates are simple vector additions, SatAnomHD can continuously refine its class HV as telemetry arrives, sustaining high TNR and suppressing false alarms without ground intervention.

This paper introduces SatAnomHD, a prediction-driven hyperdimensional computing framework that forecasts future telemetry trajectories and classifies predicted samples to detect anomalies minutes before they are observed with gradient-free HDC operations, enabling efficient inference and on-board continual fine-tuning as the mission evolves. Across prediction horizons from 30 seconds to 5 minutes, SatAnomHD achieves alarm precision that matches Telemanom-ESA, while delivering up to 60× faster inference and 206× energy-efficient training, demonstrating that predictive HDC inference offers a practically deployable path to early fault response without sacrificing alarm reliability.

Although SatAnomHD improves precision at longer prediction horizons, recall remains 0.055 for all evaluated horizons, motivating richer representations of the heterogeneous anomaly class. Future work will investigate lightweight HDC ensembles composed of multiple classifier heads that specialize on distinct anomaly regimes while sharing the same encoder and forecaster, building on multi-model HDC inference composition frameworks [40]. A complementary direction is an FPGA implementation of the encoder, forecaster, and classifier, using existing computational-reuse techniques and low-power HDC architectures as a starting point [41, 42]. The design will reuse computation across consecutive overlapping telemetry windows and support the existing online Kalman-style updates using fixed-point arithmetic [42]. Because software inference already requires only 0.21–0.52 ms at an approximately 30 s sampling interval, evaluation will emphasize energy per telemetry window, duty-cycled active and idle power, and accuracy across operating temperatures rather than peak throughput alone, following flightoriented onboard FPGA studies and thermal-aware FPGA design methods [43, 44].
